symptoms_not_in_common: Migrating nodules are not characteristic

Ultrasonography did not describe a characteristic cystic lesion

http_response.description: 66-year-old man with progressive neurologic symptoms beginning around 2000, including unexplained falls while riding a motorcycle. By October 2003, he developed blurred vision, photophobia, and worsening imbalance/unsteadiness while walking. He had bilateral cataracts and presbyopia treated with bilateral lens implantation in 2000 without benefit. Examination showed irregular pupils with sluggish direct light reflexes, slow and limited vertical gaze, slow horizontal pursuit with bilateral adduction paresis, normal convergence, impaired rapid alternating movements, and a tendency to fall backward. Over time, he developed frequent falls requiring a cane, retrocollis, slurred speech, inability to look down, and dysphagia. By March 2007, he was admitted for dysphagia with repeated aspiration; exam showed fixed up- and outward-deviated eyes with absent vertical and medial eye movements, no convergence, no Bell’s phenomenon, no optokinetic or caloric nystagmus, absent doll’s eye responses, severe nuchal rigidity, inability to sit independently, backward falls, axial rigidity, symmetric minimally brisk reflexes, flexor plantar responses, and no resting tremor.

data.description: A progressive neurodegenerative tauopathy characterized by early backward falls, vertical gaze palsy, axial rigidity, and bulbar dysfunction. This is the strongest fit; advanced disease can progress beyond a purely supranuclear eye movement disorder.
symptoms_in_common: Early, progressive imbalance and frequent backward falls
Slow vertical eye movements progressing to inability to look down
Retrocollis, severe nuchal rigidity, and axial rigidity
Slurred speech and severe dysphagia with repeated aspiration
symptoms_not_in_common: Irregular pupils with sluggish light reflexes are not characteristic
Complete loss of vestibulo-ocular responses is atypical early in the disease, although it can occur in advanced disease
Fixed upward and outward eye deviation is an unusual advanced presentation

data.description: An inherited progressive neurodegenerative disorder that can cause gait ataxia, slow eye movements, external ophthalmoplegia, dysarthria, dysphagia, and rigidity.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive restriction of eye movements and eventual ophthalmoplegia
symptoms_not_in_common: Early backward falls with pronounced axial rigidity and retrocollis are more characteristic of progressive supranuclear palsy
Prominent early vertical gaze impairment is less typical than broader cerebellar and ocular motor dysfunction
Irregular, poorly light-reactive pupils are not a defining feature

data.description: A progressive synucleinopathy combining autonomic failure with parkinsonism, cerebellar dysfunction, or both. It can cause rapid deterioration in gait, speech, and swallowing.
symptoms_in_common: Absence of a typical resting tremor
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe vertical gaze palsy and progressive complete ophthalmoplegia strongly argue against this diagnosis
Retrocollis is less characteristic than the forward neck flexion often seen in multiple system atrophy
Early predominant backward falls are more suggestive of progressive supranuclear palsy
Irregular pupils and fixed upward and outward eye deviation are not characteristic

data.diagnosis: Corticobasal degeneration presenting as a progressive supranuclear palsy syndrome
data.description: A neurodegenerative tauopathy usually associated with asymmetric rigidity, limb apraxia, and cortical dysfunction, but occasionally presenting with a progressive supranuclear palsy-like syndrome.
symptoms_not_in_common: The predominantly symmetric axial syndrome is less typical than asymmetric limb involvement
Extensive ophthalmoplegia with absent vestibulo-ocular responses is unusual
Irregular pupils with sluggish light reflexes are not characteristic
Early backward falls and retrocollis favor progressive supranuclear palsy

data.description: A rare, potentially treatable infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei that can involve the brain and mimic progressive supranuclear palsy, sometimes without gastrointestinal manifestations.
symptoms_not_in_common: The dominant combination of early backward falls, retrocollis, and axial rigidity is more typical of progressive supranuclear palsy
Fixed upward and outward eye deviation with widespread loss of ocular reflexes is not a characteristic presentation
Irregular pupils with sluggish light responses are nonspecific rather than a typical diagnostic feature

http_response.description: A 36-year-old man, sexually active with men, presented to the emergency department with a 2-week history of fever, headache, drowsiness, and photophobia. He was previously healthy. Physical examination revealed a temperature of 38.3°C and neck stiffness. CT of the head was normal. Lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 29 cm of water (ref: <20 cm). CSF analysis revealed: cell count 340 cells/µL (90% mononuclear cells, predominantly lymphocytes), glucose 46 mg/dL, and protein 0.80 g/L. HIV antibody test was positive with viral load 300,000 copies/mL and CD4+ count of 7 cells/µL.

data.description: An opportunistic fungal infection of the meninges, most commonly caused by Cryptococcus neoformans. This is the leading consideration given advanced HIV, subacute symptoms, and elevated intracranial pressure.
symptoms_in_common: Two-week history of fever and headache
Elevated CSF opening pressure of 29 cm of water
Lymphocyte-predominant CSF inflammation and elevated protein
Profound immunosuppression with a CD4+ count of 7 cells/µL
Normal head CT, which does not exclude meningitis
symptoms_not_in_common: The CSF cell count of 340 cells/µL is higher than typically seen in cryptococcal meningitis associated with profound HIV-related immunosuppression

data.description: A subacute infection of the meninges caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, with increased risk in advanced HIV.
symptoms_not_in_common: CSF glucose of 46 mg/dL is not markedly reduced, although interpretation requires a paired serum glucose
CSF protein of 0.80 g/L is less elevated than often seen in established tuberculous meningitis

data.description: An opportunistic viral infection of the brain and meninges, usually occurring in people with HIV and CD4+ counts below 50 cells/µL.
symptoms_not_in_common: A predominantly meningitic presentation with prominent neck stiffness and photophobia is less typical than progressive encephalopathy or ventriculoencephalitis
Marked lymphocyte-predominant pleocytosis is less characteristic of CMV ventriculoencephalitis, which may produce neutrophilic CSF inflammation

data.description: A viral infection of the meninges that can accompany newly acquired or recurrent HSV-2 infection and may be more severe in immunocompromised patients.
symptoms_in_common: Fever, headache, photophobia, and neck stiffness
symptoms_not_in_common: Drowsiness is less typical of uncomplicated HSV-2 meningitis and suggests encephalitic involvement or another cause
Elevated intracranial pressure is less characteristic than in cryptococcal meningitis

data.diagnosis: Early neurosyphilis presenting as syphilitic meningitis
data.description: Central nervous system infection by Treponema pallidum that can cause meningitis during early syphilis; HIV coinfection increases clinical concern.
symptoms_in_common: Sexual exposure context associated with increased syphilis risk
Subacute headache, fever, photophobia, and neck stiffness
Lymphocyte-predominant CSF pleocytosis and elevated protein
symptoms_not_in_common: Drowsiness is less typical of isolated early syphilitic meningitis
Elevated CSF opening pressure is possible but less characteristic than in cryptococcal meningitis

http_response.description: An 83-year-old woman presented to the acute stroke unit with sudden onset double vision that had lasted for three hours. She had a medical history of monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance and atrial fibrillation, for which she was not receiving anticoagulation because of an adverse reaction to warfarin. She had no history of transient ischaemic attack or stroke. She had diplopia only when looking through her right eye. On examination, she was unable to adduct her left eye, with nystagmus in her right eye when she attempted to do this. Her neurological examination was otherwise normal.

data.diagnosis: Acute brainstem ischemic stroke causing left internuclear ophthalmoplegia
data.description: The leading diagnosis is a small infarction affecting the left medial longitudinal fasciculus in the pons or midbrain. Sudden onset and atrial fibrillation without anticoagulation strongly support ischemia; urgent stroke assessment is warranted.
symptoms_in_common: Sudden-onset diplopia persisting for three hours
Inability to adduct the left eye
Right-eye abducting nystagmus during attempted left-eye adduction
Otherwise normal neurological examination, compatible with an isolated small brainstem infarction
symptoms_not_in_common: Diplopia reportedly present only when viewing through the right eye; if truly monocular, this is not explained by internuclear ophthalmoplegia and requires clarification

data.description: Demyelination of the medial longitudinal fasciculus, most commonly associated with multiple sclerosis, can disrupt coordinated horizontal eye movements. A first presentation at age 83 is highly unusual.
symptoms_not_in_common: Abrupt onset is more suggestive of ischemia than inflammatory demyelination
Reported right-eye monocular diplopia is not characteristic

data.diagnosis: Ocular myasthenia gravis with pseudo-internuclear ophthalmoplegia
data.description: Autoimmune dysfunction of neuromuscular transmission can cause variable extraocular muscle weakness and occasionally mimic internuclear ophthalmoplegia.
symptoms_in_common: Contralateral abducting nystagmus can occasionally occur in a pseudo-internuclear ophthalmoplegia pattern
symptoms_not_in_common: Sudden onset without reported fluctuation or fatigability is less typical
Reported right-eye monocular diplopia is not characteristic

data.description: A partial third cranial nerve palsy can weaken the left medial rectus muscle and impair adduction, although the paired finding of contralateral abducting nystagmus favors internuclear ophthalmoplegia.
symptoms_in_common: Inability to adduct the left eye
symptoms_not_in_common: Right-eye abducting nystagmus is not a typical feature
An isolated adduction deficit without reported ptosis or other third-nerve deficits is less typical
Reported right-eye monocular diplopia is not explained by a left oculomotor palsy

data.description: An optical abnormality such as cataract, irregular astigmatism, or tear-film disturbance can cause double vision that persists when the affected eye views alone. It would not explain the neurological eye-movement findings and could only be a concurrent condition or reflect ambiguity in the history.
symptoms_in_common: Diplopia reportedly occurring when viewing through the right eye alone
symptoms_not_in_common: Inability to adduct the left eye
Right-eye abducting nystagmus
Sudden onset is less typical for chronic optical causes such as cataract

http_response.description: 35-day-old male infant, born at 37.5 weeks as a fraternal twin by cesarean section for breech presentation, previously healthy and fed breast milk plus formula, presented with 2 days of worsening fussiness, pallor, fever, vomiting, mottled skin, and respiratory distress. The day before admission he was noted to be pale and warm with one episode of vomiting; on admission he had tachycardia and increased vomiting. Exam showed temperature 39.1°C, pulse 176/min, respiratory rate 68/min with retractions, oxygen saturation 97% on 1 L nasal cannula, pallor, listlessness, mottled cool extremities, a grade 2/6 holosystolic-flow murmur, and splenomegaly 2–3 cm below the costal margin. Urinalysis showed dark red cloudy urine with blood, protein, and granular casts.

data.description: A parasitic infection of red blood cells that can rarely be transmitted congenitally and present weeks after birth. Severe disease causes hemolytic anemia and organ dysfunction; confirmation requires blood smear or PCR.
symptoms_in_common: Dark red urine potentially reflecting hemoglobinuria from hemolysis
Tachycardia and a flow murmur potentially related to anemia
Listlessness, respiratory distress, and poor peripheral perfusion
symptoms_not_in_common: No major clinical feature is incompatible, although granular casts and proteinuria suggest renal involvement rather than uncomplicated infection

data.diagnosis: Late-onset neonatal bacterial sepsis, potentially from a urinary source
data.description: An invasive bacterial infection in a young infant that can rapidly cause shock, respiratory distress, and kidney injury. This presentation requires immediate emergency evaluation and treatment.
symptoms_in_common: Mottled, cool extremities and pallor suggesting poor perfusion
Blood, protein, and granular casts in urine potentially indicating kidney injury
symptoms_not_in_common: Splenomegaly is less typical of an acute, short-duration bacterial infection
Dark red urine and pronounced pallor together raise concern for hemolysis beyond uncomplicated sepsis

data.description: A maternally transmitted Plasmodium infection that may become symptomatic several weeks after birth, producing fever, hemolytic anemia, and splenomegaly. Likelihood depends strongly on maternal residence or travel in a malaria-endemic region.
symptoms_in_common: Presentation at approximately five weeks of age
Dark urine potentially reflecting severe hemolysis
symptoms_not_in_common: Granular casts and proteinuria are not typical of uncomplicated congenital malaria, although severe infection can cause kidney injury

data.diagnosis: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency with acute hemolysis
data.description: An inherited red-cell enzyme deficiency, most often clinically apparent in males, that can cause acute hemolysis during infection or after oxidant exposure.
symptoms_in_common: Dark red urine potentially representing hemoglobinuria
Tachycardia and a flow murmur potentially caused by anemia
Urinary granular casts and protein potentially reflecting pigment-associated kidney injury
symptoms_not_in_common: High fever would suggest a triggering infection rather than the enzyme deficiency itself
Splenomegaly is less characteristic of an isolated acute G6PD-related hemolytic episode

data.diagnosis: Hereditary spherocytosis with an infection-associated hemolytic crisis
data.description: An inherited red-cell membrane disorder causing splenic destruction of red blood cells and anemia, which can worsen during infection and occasionally present in early infancy.
symptoms_in_common: Tachycardia and a flow murmur potentially related to anemia
Listlessness and respiratory distress during severe anemia
symptoms_not_in_common: High fever and vomiting require an associated infection or another explanation
Dark red urine suggesting hemoglobinuria is less typical because hemolysis is predominantly extravascular
Proteinuria and granular casts are not usual primary manifestations

http_response.description: 70-year-old man with history of Gleason 9 (4+5) adenocarcinoma treated with radical prostatectomy 10 years ago. Presented to primary care with rectal pain persisting for several weeks. Patient had lost 20 lbs over 3-4 weeks and complained of progressive fatigue, poor appetite, severe tenesmus, and rectal pain. Patient had been living independently on West Coast but relocated to East Coast to be closer to adult children.

data.diagnosis: Recurrent prostate adenocarcinoma with pelvic or rectal involvement
data.description: High-grade prostate cancer can recur years after prostatectomy and invade or compress nearby pelvic structures, including the rectum. The prior Gleason 9 tumor makes recurrence an important concern requiring prompt evaluation.
symptoms_in_common: Severe tenesmus from possible rectal compression or invasion
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe rectal symptoms are an uncommon presentation of prostate cancer recurrence unless there is substantial local pelvic involvement

data.description: A malignant tumor of the rectal lining that can cause a persistent urge to defecate, rectal discomfort, and systemic symptoms, particularly in advanced disease.
A malignancy of the anal canal that may cause persistent anorectal pain and, when locally advanced, obstructive symptoms and weight loss.
symptoms_in_common: Severe tenesmus with possible anal canal or adjacent rectal involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked weight loss over only 3–4 weeks is less typical of localized anal cancer

data.description: A malignancy of lymphoid tissue that can rarely involve the rectum or form a pelvic mass, producing local pressure symptoms and systemic illness.
symptoms_in_common: Rectal pain from possible rectal or pelvic involvement
Tenesmus from possible rectal compression or infiltration
symptoms_not_in_common: Rectal pain and severe tenesmus are uncommon lymphoma presentations unless the rectum or adjacent pelvic structures are involved

data.description: An infection forming a collection of pus around the rectum or anus; a deep abscess may cause persistent rectal pain and pressure without obvious external swelling.
symptoms_not_in_common: A 20-pound weight loss over 3–4 weeks is atypical for an uncomplicated anorectal abscess

http_response.description: 27-year-old man with 3 days of upper leg myalgias followed by acute worsening weakness on presentation, unable to lift legs or stand, with associated arm weakness. For several months he had insomnia, loose stools, ~5 kg weight loss, and hand tremor. He started an herbal stress supplement 4 days before presentation. Exam showed bilateral conjunctival injection, proximal weakness (4/5 upper extremities, 3/5 lower extremities), brisk patellar reflexes, and fine hand tremor. Labs revealed severe hypokalemia (K 1.8 mmol/L), mild transaminitis, elevated alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin, elevated CK and aldolase, and venous pH 7.29.

data.diagnosis: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis, potentially due to Graves disease
data.description: The leading possibility: excess thyroid hormone promotes potassium movement into cells, causing profound hypokalemia and acute weakness, especially in young men. Thyroid testing is needed for confirmation. Potassium of 1.8 mmol/L with paralysis requires emergency cardiac monitoring and treatment.
symptoms_in_common: Acute severe proximal weakness affecting the legs more than the arms
Months of weight loss, loose stools, insomnia, and fine hand tremor suggesting thyrotoxicosis
Brisk reflexes, which can reflect underlying thyrotoxicosis
Liver biochemical abnormalities, which can accompany thyrotoxicosis
symptoms_not_in_common: Venous acidemia is atypical for an isolated intracellular potassium shift
Brisk reflexes are less typical during the paralytic episode itself
Conjunctival injection alone is nonspecific and does not establish Graves eye disease

data.description: An herbal product could cause potassium depletion or redistribution through laxative, stimulant, thyroid-active, or other ingredients. The temporal association warrants ingredient review but does not establish causation.
symptoms_in_common: Supplement initiation shortly before the acute illness
Severe hypokalemia with generalized proximal weakness
Myalgias and elevated CK and aldolase, compatible with hypokalemic muscle injury
Loose stools, which could contribute to potassium loss if worsened by the supplement
Abnormal liver tests, which can occur with some supplement toxicities
symptoms_not_in_common: Weight loss, tremor, insomnia, and loose stools began months before supplement use
Conjunctival injection is not a characteristic finding
Acidemia is not typical of licorice-mediated potassium loss, which generally causes metabolic alkalosis

data.description: An inherited skeletal-muscle ion-channel disorder causing episodic weakness from potassium redistribution into cells. A first recognized attack can occur in a young adult, although secondary causes must be excluded.
symptoms_in_common: Acute marked limb weakness with lower-limb predominance
Elevated CK, which can occur during attacks
symptoms_not_in_common: Persistent weight loss, loose stools, insomnia, and tremor suggest a secondary endocrine cause
Brisk patellar reflexes are atypical during an attack
Venous acidemia is not characteristic
Liver biochemical abnormalities and conjunctival injection are not characteristic

data.diagnosis: Renal tubular acidosis causing hypokalemic paralysis
data.description: A renal acid-handling disorder, particularly distal renal tubular acidosis, can produce metabolic acidosis and substantial urinary potassium loss, resulting in paralysis. Confirmation requires bicarbonate, anion gap, and urine studies.
symptoms_in_common: Venous acidemia, if attributable to metabolic acidosis
Myalgias and elevated muscle enzymes from potassium depletion
symptoms_not_in_common: Months of tremor, insomnia, weight loss, and loose stools are not explained well
Brisk reflexes are not characteristic of severe hypokalemic paralysis
Conjunctival injection and liver biochemical abnormalities are not typical

data.description: Excess thyroid hormone can cause proximal muscle weakness and wasting, usually developing gradually. It could coexist with hypokalemic periodic paralysis but would not adequately explain the abrupt episode alone.
symptoms_in_common: Proximal weakness involving both upper and lower extremities
Weight loss, insomnia, loose stools, and fine hand tremor
Liver biochemical abnormalities compatible with thyrotoxicosis
symptoms_not_in_common: Abrupt inability to stand is less typical than gradually progressive weakness
Profound hypokalemia is not explained by uncomplicated thyrotoxic myopathy
Myalgias and elevated CK and aldolase are less typical because muscle enzymes are often normal
Venous acidemia is not characteristic

http_response.description: A 70-year-old woman presented to the clinic for a routine examination. The patient reported that this mass had been present since birth. Her symptoms were minimal, with occasional difficulty cleaning the area and halitosis from entrapped food, but she was otherwise asymptomatic regarding the lesion.

data.description: A congenital fold of excess tissue on the inner lip that may trap food and interfere with oral hygiene. This is a possibility if the mass involves the lip; its location was not provided.
A benign bony prominence along the midline of the hard palate, usually requiring no treatment unless it interferes with oral function or hygiene.
symptoms_in_common: Food entrapment that can contribute to halitosis
symptoms_not_in_common: Reported presence since birth is less typical; these growths usually become apparent later

data.description: A benign developmental overgrowth of tissues normally found in the mouth, potentially involving the tongue or adjacent structures.
symptoms_in_common: Potential interference with cleaning and food clearance
symptoms_not_in_common: Halitosis is not a characteristic primary symptom, although it may result from trapped food

data.description: A congenital malformation of lymphatic vessels that can produce a painless oral swelling, commonly involving the tongue.
symptoms_in_common: Possible difficulty cleaning and food retention around an irregular surface
symptoms_not_in_common: Halitosis is not a characteristic primary symptom
An otherwise asymptomatic course into late adulthood is less typical of extensive oral lesions

http_response.description: A 52-year-old woman presented with a two-day history of lower back pain radiating into her left leg with associated leg weakness. She had a history of chronic back pain. Neurological examination revealed reduced power in her left leg (3/5), but was otherwise normal.

data.diagnosis: Lumbar disc herniation with left-sided radiculopathy
data.description: A herniated lumbar disc compresses a nerve root, causing radiating leg pain and potentially focal weakness. This is the most likely explanation; new weakness of approximately 3/5 warrants urgent assessment and lumbar MRI.
symptoms_in_common: Lower back pain radiating into the left leg
Acute symptoms superimposed on chronic back pain
Otherwise normal neurological examination, compatible with focal nerve-root involvement

data.description: Degenerative narrowing of the spinal canal or neural foramina can compress lumbar nerves, causing back pain, radiating leg pain, and weakness.
symptoms_in_common: Pain radiating into the left leg
symptoms_not_in_common: An abrupt two-day presentation with substantial weakness is less typical than gradually progressive or activity-dependent symptoms

data.description: Slippage of one lumbar vertebra relative to another can produce mechanical back pain and narrow the spaces through which nerve roots pass.
symptoms_in_common: Lower back pain radiating into one leg
Focal leg weakness from possible nerve-root compression
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute development of marked weakness over two days is less typical of uncomplicated degenerative vertebral slippage

data.diagnosis: Lumbar facet joint synovial cyst causing radiculopathy
data.description: A cyst arising from a degenerative lumbar facet joint can compress an adjacent nerve root. Enlargement or bleeding into the cyst can occasionally cause sudden symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Reduced power in the affected leg
symptoms_not_in_common: Rapid onset over two days is less typical unless the cyst acutely enlarges or bleeds

diagnoses.name: Intervertebral disc prolapse
diagnoses.title: Intervertebral disc degeneration without prolapsed disc with determinant

http_response.description: A 52-year-old Korean man presented with a 1-month history of general weakness that was aggravated three days before his emergency room visit. Initial neurologic examination revealed disorientation of time, place, and person, attention deficit, immediate memory disturbance, dysarthria, weakness of bilateral upper extremities with increased deep tendon reflexes, and right hemiparetic gait. Blood work showed an elevated eosinophil count of 5,500/μL, representing 41% of total white blood cells. The patient's clinical history and basic examinations did not reveal any identifiable cause of hypereosinophilia, including parasitic infection, neoplasm, vasculitis, or allergy. Additionally, the patient had no prior clinical symptoms or signs suggesting Churg-Strauss syndrome, such as sinusitis or asthma. Cardiac enzymes were elevated with creatine kinase-MB at 7.3 ng/ml and troponin-I at 4.78 ng/ml. An echocardiogram revealed mild left ventricular inferior wall hypokinesia.

data.diagnosis: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome with neurologic and cardiac involvement
data.description: A leading consideration characterized by marked, otherwise unexplained eosinophilia with eosinophil-mediated organ injury. Neurologic dysfunction can result from cerebral thrombosis, embolism, or direct tissue injury. Confirmation requires further exclusion of secondary and clonal causes.
symptoms_in_common: Marked eosinophilia of 5,500/μL, representing 41% of white blood cells
Disorientation, attention deficit, and immediate memory disturbance
Dysarthria, bilateral upper-extremity weakness, increased deep tendon reflexes, and right hemiparetic gait
Elevated cardiac enzymes and left ventricular inferior wall hypokinesia
No identifiable secondary cause of hypereosinophilia on the initial evaluation

data.diagnosis: Eosinophilic myocarditis or endomyocarditis with cardioembolic cerebral ischemia
data.description: Eosinophilic cardiac inflammation can cause myocardial injury and endocardial thrombosis, potentially producing cerebral emboli. This could explain the combined cardiac and neurologic findings, although brain imaging, further cardiac imaging, and possibly biopsy are needed.
symptoms_in_common: Dysarthria and right hemiparetic gait compatible with cerebral ischemia
Cognitive dysfunction potentially attributable to multifocal cerebral injury
symptoms_not_in_common: Neurologic deficits are not typical of isolated myocarditis without an embolic or other vascular complication

data.diagnosis: Clonal hypereosinophilia due to a myeloid neoplasm
data.description: A hematologic disorder, such as chronic eosinophilic leukemia or a myeloid neoplasm with an eosinophilia-associated kinase fusion, can cause persistent eosinophilia and cardiac or neurologic organ injury. A normal basic neoplasm evaluation does not exclude these disorders; molecular and bone marrow testing may be necessary.
symptoms_in_common: Possible thrombotic or eosinophil-mediated neurologic injury
symptoms_not_in_common: No neoplasm was identified during the initial evaluation
The acute focal neurologic deficits would require a vascular or organ-injury complication rather than uncomplicated marrow disease

data.description: An eosinophilic small- and medium-vessel vasculitis, formerly called Churg-Strauss syndrome, usually associated with asthma and sinonasal disease. It may affect the heart and nervous system, but this presentation lacks several characteristic features.
symptoms_in_common: Possible cardiac inflammation indicated by elevated cardiac enzymes and ventricular hypokinesia
Neurologic dysfunction potentially caused by vascular injury
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of asthma or sinusitis
No evidence of vasculitis on the initial evaluation
Increased reflexes and hemiparetic gait indicate central nervous system involvement rather than the more characteristic peripheral neuropathy

data.diagnosis: Tissue-invasive helminth infection with secondary hypereosinophilia
data.description: Certain parasitic infections can cause profound eosinophilia and, less commonly, cardiac or central nervous system injury. This is a lower-probability alternative because the initial assessment found no parasitic cause; its relevance depends on exposure history and targeted testing.
symptoms_in_common: Neurologic abnormalities potentially compatible with central nervous system involvement
Myocardial injury potentially compatible with parasitic or eosinophilic myocarditis
symptoms_not_in_common: No parasitic infection was identified during the initial evaluation
The combination of focal upper motor neuron deficits and myocardial injury is uncommon in most helminth infections

http_response.description: A 44-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer presented with abnormal findings on 18-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography imaging. She had previously been diagnosed with breast cancer (T1N2M0, Stage IIIa, intraductal carcinoma, triple negative cancer) and had undergone adjuvant chemotherapy and radiation therapy after a right breast conserving surgery 2 years prior. She was a non-smoker with no specific occupational or environmental exposure to known carcinogens and had been taking tamoxifen after chemotherapy. Laboratory results revealed mild anemia (hemoglobin 11.4 mg/dL) and leucopenia (3,300/μL), with all other results within normal limits. Additional laboratory findings included an elevated angiotensin I-converting enzyme level of 101 U/L, and her purified protein derivative skin test for tuberculosis was negative. The biopsy sample was also negative for tuberculosis antigen-specific interferon gamma.

data.description: A systemic inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas. It can produce FDG-avid lesions that resemble cancer recurrence; biopsy and exclusion of infectious causes are needed for confirmation.
symptoms_in_common: Mild anemia and leukopenia can occur with systemic involvement
Negative tuberculosis testing supports consideration of a non-tuberculous granulomatous process
symptoms_not_in_common: No clearly atypical finding is provided, although the PET distribution and biopsy histology are not described

data.description: A noncaseating granulomatous reaction associated with cancer or its treatment, without necessarily meeting criteria for systemic sarcoidosis. It can mimic metastatic disease on FDG-PET.
symptoms_not_in_common: Mild anemia and leukopenia are not characteristic of an isolated sarcoid-like reaction

data.description: Return or distant spread of previously treated breast cancer. Her prior node-positive, stage IIIA disease makes recurrence an important possibility, but FDG uptake alone cannot establish it.
symptoms_in_common: History of stage IIIA breast cancer
Abnormal FDG-PET findings two years after treatment
Mild anemia and leukopenia could occur with marrow involvement, although they are nonspecific
symptoms_not_in_common: Elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme level is not a typical marker of breast cancer recurrence

data.description: A malignancy of lymphocytes that commonly produces FDG-avid disease and can cause cytopenias through marrow or splenic involvement.
symptoms_not_in_common: Elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme level is not characteristic, although it can occasionally occur

data.description: An infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis that can produce granulomatous, FDG-avid lesions resembling sarcoidosis or malignancy. Negative immune-based tests reduce suspicion but do not completely exclude active infection.
symptoms_in_common: Mild anemia can accompany chronic infection
Leukopenia can occur in disseminated disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Negative purified protein derivative skin test
Reported negative tuberculosis antigen-specific interferon-gamma testing
Elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme level is less characteristic than in sarcoidosis

http_response.description: 78-year-old woman with 2 months of lethargy and easy fatigue, referred for anemia with elevated ESR. Past history: hypertension and hypercholesterolemia, treated with perindopril and atorvastatin. Examination was normal, with no organomegaly or lymphadenopathy; ECOG performance status 1. Blood tests showed anemia (Hb 99 g/L), elevated ESR (120 mm/h), mildly raised creatinine and calcium, and mildly increased LDH. Further studies revealed IgG kappa paraprotein, elevated β₂-microglobulin, markedly increased free kappa light chains with high kappa/lambda ratio, and urinary kappa Bence-Jones protein; 24-hour urine protein was normal.

data.description: A malignancy of clonal plasma cells producing monoclonal immunoglobulin and/or light chains. This is the leading consideration, although confirmation requires bone marrow assessment and evaluation of myeloma-defining findings.
symptoms_in_common: Markedly increased free kappa light chains and high kappa/lambda ratio
Elevated beta-2-microglobulin and mildly increased LDH
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported bone pain or documented bone lesions, although these are not required
Normal 24-hour urine protein despite detectable urinary monoclonal light chains

data.description: An asymptomatic clonal plasma-cell disorder with a substantial monoclonal protein level or marrow plasma-cell burden but no myeloma-defining events. It remains possible only if the anemia and biochemical abnormalities are unrelated and the free light-chain findings do not meet a myeloma-defining threshold.
symptoms_in_common: Increased free kappa light chains and abnormal kappa/lambda ratio
symptoms_not_in_common: Anemia with hemoglobin 99 g/L, if attributable to the plasma-cell disorder
Lethargy and easy fatigue potentially reflecting disease-related anemia
Raised creatinine and calcium, if sufficiently elevated and attributable to the disorder
Marked free light-chain abnormality, which could itself meet a myeloma-defining threshold depending on the exact values

data.description: A clonal plasma-cell condition with a limited monoclonal protein and marrow plasma-cell burden, without attributable organ damage. The current findings are more concerning for myeloma, but this remains a consideration if the anemia and other abnormalities have separate causes.
symptoms_not_in_common: Anemia with hemoglobin 99 g/L

http_response.description: 7-day-old female newborn born at full-term to a G1P1 mother with birth weight of 4,380 gm. Parents denied poor feeding, poor activity, or weak crying. On examination at Day 7, she had normal muscle power, normal reflex, no macroglossia, but slightly decreased facial folds. Newborn screening for Pompe disease showed GAA activity 0.18 uM/h (critical cutoff <0.5) and ratio 42.87 (critical cutoff acid β-glucosidase/GAA ≥20). Laboratory examination revealed elevated pro-BNP (8,738 pg/mL), CK (722 U/L), and ALT (112 U/L). Confirmatory testing showed deficient lymphocyte GAA activity (1.33 nmol/g pro/hr, normal mean 66.7). Patient did not have the common CRIM-positive Taiwan Pompe disease p.D645E variant. Mutation analysis revealed heterozygous c.2024_2026del (p.N675del) and c.2040+1G>T variants in trans.

data.diagnosis: Infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II)
data.description: The strongly favored diagnosis: an autosomal recessive deficiency of lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA) causing glycogen accumulation, particularly in cardiac and skeletal muscle. Markedly deficient GAA activity and two GAA variants in trans support Pompe disease; elevated pro-BNP raises concern for early cardiac involvement, requiring echocardiographic assessment. Absence of p.D645E does not establish CRIM status.

Severely deficient confirmatory lymphocyte GAA activity
Two GAA variants identified in trans
Elevated pro-BNP suggesting possible cardiac involvement
Elevated CK consistent with muscle injury
Elevated ALT, which can accompany muscle involvement
Slightly decreased facial folds, potentially reflecting subtle facial muscle involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal muscle power and reflexes, unlike established symptomatic infantile disease
No poor feeding, reduced activity, or weak crying
No macroglossia; however, absence of these findings at seven days does not exclude infantile-onset disease

Normal neonatal muscle power and reflexes

http_response.description: An 81-year-old man presented to the ICU 10 days after a 4-week cruise in New Caledonia, Vanuatu, the Solomon Islands, and New Zealand.
